name: feature-carousel
title: Feature carousel
description: Feature cards on native scroll snapping with the next card peeking, a counter and arrows, for many features in little room.
docs: Pass title, an optional description and eyebrow, items (an id, an image or an icon, a title, a line and an optional href) and cardWidth (in px, 320 by default). The cards sit on native scroll snapping, so a swipe on a phone and the trackpad on a laptop feel right. The next card always shows by about a quarter of its width: where the width would hide it, or show it nearly whole and cut, the cards are resized a little to make it so. Because the server cannot know the width, the row waits, hidden, until the page has fitted the cards and then fades in, so it never visibly changes size; without scripting it is shown as it is. Pass bleed (a number of px or a CSS length such as "1.5rem" or "var(--page-gutter)", 0 by default) as your page's side padding and the row runs on past the block, so the card that peeks goes off the edge of the screen on a phone instead of stopping at the margin; a variable lets it be 0 where the page has margin to spare. The heading and the Previous and Next buttons share one row where they fit: a short title keeps them beside it on a phone, and a long one sends them to a row of their own below it. The counter ("3 of 8") counts the last card fully in view and follows the real scroll position whether the reader used the buttons, a swipe or the keyboard. It is said politely as it changes, but only once the reader has moved the row, so opening the page announces nothing. The buttons dim at the ends but stay focusable, so keyboard focus is never lost. While the row has focus the arrow keys move one card and Home and End go to the ends; every link inside stays in the tab order. Nothing autoplays, and under reduced motion scrolling is instant. A card with an image shows it in a 16:10 frame; one with an icon and no image gets a tile. A card with an href is a whole-card link named after its title. labels translates the fixed words.
